parole.significato: A producer of something, or an agent in the production of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -gène, from the Ancient Greek -γενής (-genḗs).

parole.significato: Something written or otherwise represented in the specified manner, or about a specified subject.
parole.testo: From French -graphie, inherited from Latin -graphia, borrowed from Ancient Greek -γραφία (-graphía), from γραφή (graphḗ, “writing, drawing, description”). By surface analysis, -graph + -y.

parole.significato: Forming compound nouns with the sense of person who has a mania for.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -mane, from Ancient Greek -μανής (-manḗs).

parole.significato: Having parts of the specified quality.
parole.testo: From French -mère and its etymon Ancient Greek -μερής (-merḗs, “having (the specified number of) parts”, “sharing”): the combining form of μέρος (méros, “part”)) with the English suffix -ous; compare the English -mer and -mere, as well as the French -mère and the German -mer.

parole.significato: Used to form the names of measuring devices.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -mètre, a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron).

parole.significato: Indicating a life-form, often microscopic
parole.testo: Abstracted from aerobe and microbe, both formed in French using the Ancient Greek word βίος (bíos, “life”).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns denoting a person having a fear of a specific thing.
parole.testo: From French -phobe, from Latin -phobus, from Attic Greek -φόβος (-phóbos), combining form of φόβος (phóbos), ablaut variant of φέβεσθαι (phébesthai), middle infinitive of φέβομαι (phébomai), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ-. Cognates include Russian бегать (begatʹ, “run, flee”), Slovak bežať (“run”)

parole.significato: exhibiting a behavior.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -tropie, from Ancient Greek -τροπίᾱ (-tropíā), from τρόπος (trópos, “a turn”).

parole.significato: A univalent radical or functional group formed from a given molecule. Thus propyl from propane, benzyl from benzene, an…
parole.testo: Via French méthylène from Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “wood, material”).

parole.significato: Having no head.
parole.testo: From French acéphale, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”). By surface analysis, a- + -cephalous.

parole.significato: An athlete who performs acts requiring skill, agility and coordination, often as part of a circus performance.
parole.testo: From French acrobate, from Ancient Greek ἀκροβάτης (akrobátēs, “walking on tiptoe, climbing aloft”), from ἀκροβατέω (akrobatéō, “to walk on tiptoe”), from ἄκρον (ákron, “highest or farthest point, mountain top, peak”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to walk, step”).

parole.significato: Living or occurring only in the presence of oxygen e.g. aerobic bacteria.
parole.testo: From French aérobie, coined in 1863 by Louis Pasteur, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + βίος (bíos, “life”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of airplane. A powered heavier-than-air aircraft with fixed wings.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aéroplane, from Ancient Greek ἀερόπλανος (aeróplanos, “wandering in air”), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + πλάνος (plános, “wandering”), equivalent to aero- + plane. First used by Joseph Pline in an 1855 patent.https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/Aircraft_Design/NeHoahlhCGMC?hl=en&gb

parole.significato: The science of utilizing plants, animals and soils for food, fuel, feed, fiber, etc.
parole.testo: From French agronomie, from agronome (“agriculturist”), from Ancient Greek ἀγρός (agrós, “field”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). By surface analysis, agro- + -nomy.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the amnion.
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from French amniotique, from Ancient Greek ἀμνίον (amníon, “vessel for collecting the blood from sacrifices”). Equivalent to amnion + -otic.

parole.significato: Any of a large group of structurally similar hydrated double silicate minerals, containing various combinations of sodi…
parole.testo: From French amphibole, coined by René Just Haüy from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβολος (amphíbolos, “ambiguous”), in reference to its many forms.

parole.significato: A nonsense verse; a rigmarole, which is meaningless despite possibly appearing to have meaning.
parole.testo: From French amphigouri, of uncertain derivation; perhaps from Ancient Greek ἀμφί (amphí) + γῦρος (gûros, “circle”) or -αγορία (-agoría, “speech”).

parole.significato: A type of winged serpent, with two bat-like wings and typically with no other limbs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amphiptère, from Ancient Greek ἀμφί (amphí, “amphi-”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”). Compare amphisbaena (French amphisbène).

parole.significato: Without oxygen; especially of an environment or organism.
parole.testo: From French anaérobie, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + βίος (bíos, “life”) + -ic. By surface analysis, an- + aerobic.

parole.significato: In which the value of a data item (such as time) is represented by a continuous(ly) variable physical quantity that can…
parole.testo: First attested in the early 19th century; from French analogue, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλογος (análogos, “proportionate”), from ἀνά (aná, “up to”) + λόγος (lógos, “ratio”). Equivalent to ana- (“functionally similar”) + -log.

parole.significato: A form of spirometer.
parole.testo: From French anapnographe, coined by the device's inventors Léon Bergeon and M. Kastus in the 1860s, from Ancient Greek ἀναπνοή (anapnoḗ, “recovery of breath; respiration”) (from ἀναπνέω (anapnéō, “to draw breath”), from ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) + πνέω (pnéō, “to breathe”)) + French -graphe (see -graph).

parole.significato: A blue or brown mineral, a form of titanium dioxide, used as a pigment.
parole.testo: From French anatase, from Ancient Greek ἀνάτασις (anátasis, “extending, extension”), named for the length of its crystals.

parole.significato: native carbonate of soda; natron
parole.testo: From French anatron, an old variant of natron, from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron, “nitre”) by way of Spanish natrón and Arabic نَطْرُون (naṭrūn).

parole.significato: A short account of a real incident or person, often humorous or interesting.
parole.testo: Late 17ᵗʰ c., from French anecdote, from Ancient Greek ἀνέκδοτος (anékdotos, “accounts unpublished”), from ἀν- (an-, “not, un-”) + ἔκδοτος (ékdotos, “published”), from ἐκδίδωμι (ekdídōmi, “I publish”), from ἐκ- (ek-, “out”) + δίδωμι (dídōmi, “I give”). Virtually identical cognates in other European

parole.significato: Building deep vertical burrows and surfacing to feed.
parole.testo: From French anécique, coined by Marcel B. Bouché, French earthworm biologist (1971), from Ancient Greek ἀνέχω (anékhō, “to rise up, emerge”).

parole.significato: Not using or containing fluid
parole.testo: From French anéroïde, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-) + νηρός (nērós, “wet, damp”).

parole.significato: The inability to feel pleasure from activities usually found enjoyable, such as exercise, hobbies, music, sexual activi…
parole.testo: From French anhédonie (coined by Ribot, 1896), from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-) + ἡδονή (hēdonḗ, “pleasure”).

parole.significato: Alienation or social instability caused by erosion of standards and values.
parole.testo: From French anomie, from Ancient Greek ἀνομία (anomía, “lawlessness”), from ἄνομος (ánomos, “lawless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). Popularized by French sociologist Émile Durkheim (1858–1917).

parole.significato: An anonymous person.
parole.testo: Coined or borrowed around 1812, from French anonyme, from Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, “without name”).

parole.significato: The pollen-bearing part of the stamen of a flower.
parole.testo: From French anthère, from Ancient Greek ἀνθηρός (anthērós, “flowery, blooming”), from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: A tricyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (an acene containing three fused rings) obtained from coal tar; used in the manufactur…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French anthracène, coined by its co-discoverer Auguste Laurent in 1837, from Ancient Greek ἄνθραξ (ánthrax, “coal”) + -ene. By surface analysis, anthrac- + -ene.

parole.significato: The science of measuring the human body to ascertain the ranges and averages of dimensions of the human form, for vario…
parole.testo: 1839, as anthropo- (“human”) + -metry (“measurement”), from French anthropométrie, from anthropo- + -métrie, from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”), influenced by Latin use.

parole.significato: A word which has the opposite meaning of another word.
parole.testo: From French antonyme (1840s and 1850s), which was modeled on earlier synonyme and influenced by the etymons of Ancient Greek ἀντωνυμία (antōnumía, “pronoun”); credit for popularization of the French loanword's naturalization into English is given principally to Charles John Smith and his 1867 book S

parole.significato: A partial or total loss of language skills due to brain damage. Usually, damage to the left perisylvian region, includi…
parole.testo: From French aphasie, from Ancient Greek ἀφασία (aphasía), from ἄφατος (áphatos, “speechless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + φάσις (phásis, “speech”). Equivalent to a- + -phasia.

parole.significato: Of a map projection: Neither conformal or equal-area.
parole.testo: From French aphylactique, probably coined by Nicolas Auguste Tissot in his 1881 book Mémoire sur la réprésentation des surfaces et les projections des cartes géographiques (Treatise on surface representations and map projections). Ultimately from a- + Ancient Greek φυλακτικός (phulaktikós, “serving

parole.significato: A brown or green variety of andradite containing manganese.
parole.testo: From French aplome, from Ancient Greek ἁπλόος (haplóos, “single, simple”). Coined by French priest and mineralogist René Just Haüy in 1801.

parole.significato: Modification of an internal vowel sound in a word or linguistic root, especially so as to establish a lexical distincti…
parole.testo: From French apophonie, from French apo- + Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”), after Ancient Greek ἀπο- (apo-, “away, from, off”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”).

parole.significato: Tending to doubt.
parole.testo: From French aporétique, from Ancient Greek ἀπορητικός (aporētikós), from ἄπορος (áporos). By surface analysis, pore + -etic.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or favouring, an aristocracy.
parole.testo: From French aristocratique, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατικός (aristokratikós). By surface analysis, aristo- + -cratic.

parole.significato: An absolute ruler with infinite power.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French autocrate, itself from Ancient Greek αὐτοκρατής (autokratḗs, “sovereign”), from αὐτο- (auto-, “self”) (combining form of αὐτός (autós)) + κράτος (krátos, “strength, power”) + -ης (-ēs). By surface analysis, auto- + -crat.

parole.significato: A theoretical nitrogen-based counterpart to liposome structures composed of acrylonitrile self-assembled membrane in a…
parole.testo: From azote (“nitrogen”) + -o- + -some (“body”), from French azote (“nitrogen”) and Ancient Greek σῶμα (sôma, “body”), a "nitrogen body", formed by analogy with liposome.

parole.significato: A mineral, barium sulphate, with the chemical formula BaSO₄.
parole.testo: Alteration of baryte, from French barote, 1782 coinage from Ancient Greek βαρύτης (barútēs, “heaviness”), from βαρύς (barús) + -της (-tēs). By surface analysis, bar- + -ite.

parole.significato: A unit of pressure under the CGS system; symbol Ba; equal to 1 dyne per square centimeter. 1 Ba = 0.1 Pa = 0.1 N/m2 = 1…
parole.testo: From French French barye, from Ancient Greek Ancient Greek βαρύς (barús, “heavy”).

parole.significato: A cupping glass to which a scarificator and an exhausting syringe are attached.
parole.testo: From the French bdellomètre, from the Ancient Greek βδέλλα (bdélla, “leech”) + the French -mètre (“-meter”), itself from the Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, “(something used to) measure”).

parole.significato: One versed in books.
parole.testo: From French bibliognoste; equivalent to biblio- (“book”), from Ancient Greek βῐβλῐ́ον (bĭblĭ́on), and γνώστης (gnṓstēs, “expert”).

parole.significato: One who "buries" books, typically by hoarding them unread, hiding them, locking them away, or otherwise shutting them u…
parole.testo: From French bibliotaphe, from biblio- + Ancient Greek τάφος (táphos, “burial, tomb”). By surface analysis biblio- + -taph.

parole.significato: A gurgling or rumbling noise produced by gas in the bowels.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French borborygme, ultimately from Ancient Greek βορβορυγμός (borborugmós, “(onomatopoeic) borborygmus”), from βορβορύζω (borborúzō, “to experience borborygmus”).

parole.significato: A system of writing using abbreviations or special characters; shorthand.
parole.testo: From French brachygraphie, from Ancient Greek βραχύς (brakhús, “short”) + -γραφία (-graphía, “writing”).

parole.significato: bromine
parole.testo: From French brome, coined from Ancient Greek βρῶμος (brômos, “stink”). Doublet of bromus.

parole.significato: A nonmetallic chemical element (symbol Br) with an atomic number of 35; one of the halogens, it is a fuming red-brown l…
parole.testo: From obsolete English brome + -ine, this word being from French brome, from Ancient Greek βρῶμος (brômos, “stink”).

parole.significato: A mix of discordant sounds; dissonance.
parole.testo: From French cacophonie, from Ancient Greek κακοφωνία (kakophōnía), from κακός (kakós, “bad”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”), equivalent to caco- + -phony.

parole.significato: The weevil Phlyctinus callosus.
parole.testo: From French calandre. Compare Dutch klander and Medieval Latin calandrus. Ultimately from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros, “cylinder”). Doublet of calender and cylinder.

parole.significato: The art or practice of writing letters and words in a decorative style; the letters and words so written.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French calligraphie, from Ancient Greek καλλιγραφία (kalligraphía, literally “pretty writing”), from κάλλος (kállos, “beauty”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to draw”).

parole.significato: The creation of charts and maps based on the layout of a territory's geography.
parole.testo: From French cartographie, from carte (“map”) (ultimately from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “map”)) + -graphie (“-graphy”) (from γράφω (gráphō, “write”)); carto- (“map”) + -graphy.

parole.significato: Disordered cenesthesia; a psychopathological symptom characterised by generalised abnormal sensations in the body.
parole.testo: First attested 1907, borrowed from French cénestopathie, coined by Ernest Dupré and Paul Camus, from Ancient Greek κοινός (koinós, “common”) + αἴσθησις (aísthēsis, “perception from the senses”) + πάθος (páthos, “suffering, misery, condition”).

parole.significato: A monument, generally in the form of an empty tomb, erected to honour the dead whose bodies lie elsewhere, especially m…
parole.testo: From French cénotaphe, from Ancient Greek κενός (kenós, “empty”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb”). By surface analysis ceno- + -taph.

parole.significato: Any mollusc of the class Cephalopoda, which includes squid, cuttlefish, octopus, nautiloids etc.
parole.testo: From French céphalopode, from Ancient Greek κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”) + ποδός (podós), genitive singular of πούς (poús, “foot, leg”). By surface analysis, cephalo- + -pod.

parole.significato: Any of several zeolite minerals that occur in basaltic rocks.
parole.testo: From French chabasie, coined by Louis-Augustin Bosc d'Antic from Ancient Greek χαβάζιος (khabázios), apparently an error for χαλάζιος (khalázios, “a kind of precious stone”) (which is probably from χάλαζα (khálaza, “hail”), due to looking like a hailstone), one of twenty species of stones mentioned

parole.significato: A member of the order Chiroptera, a bat
parole.testo: Coined by William Whewell in 1840 as an adaptation of Cuvier's coinage, French chiroptère, from Ancient Greek χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”), equivalent to chiro- + -pter.

parole.significato: The art of creating, arranging and recording the dance movements of a work, such as a ballet.
parole.testo: Reshaping of earlier choregraphy, a borrowing from French chorégraphie, from Ancient Greek χορεία (khoreía, “dance”) + -γραφίᾱ (-graphíā, “written form (of a word, etc.), spelling”). By surface analysis, choreo- + -graphy. Both choregraphy and choreography replaced earlier chorography in the dance s

parole.significato: Chromium, when used to plate other metals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chrome.

parole.significato: A device for measuring time, particularly a precision mechanism for measuring time of day.
parole.testo: From chrono- + -meter, possibly after the model of earlier French chronomètre (“metronome”), ultimately from Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) + μέτρον (métron, “meter, measuring device”).

parole.significato: The science of risk analysis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cindyniques + English -ics (suffix forming nouns denoting fields of knowledge or practice). Cindyniques is a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κῐ́νδῡνος (kĭ́ndūnos, “danger, hazard, risk”) (probably from Pre-Greek) + French -ique (suffix forming nouns denoting fields of knowl

parole.significato: Severe pains that grip the abdomen or the disease that causes such pains (due to intestinal or bowel-related problems).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French colique. Ultimately derived from Ancient Greek κωλικός (kōlikós, “suffering in the colon”, adjective).

parole.significato: The main structural protein in the extracellular matrix of the connective tissues of many animals.
parole.testo: From French collagène, coined from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”) and -γενής (-genḗs, “-forming”) (see -gen); it is the main substance that animal glues are derived from.

parole.significato: Imparting or improving beauty, particularly the beauty of the complexion.
parole.testo: From French cosmétique, from Ancient Greek κοσμητική (kosmētikḗ, “the art of dress and ornament”), κοσμητικός (kosmētikós), from κοσμητής (kosmētḗs, “orderer, director, decorator”), from κοσμέω (kosméō, “to order, to arrange, to rule, to adorn, to equip, to dress, to embellish”), from κόσμος (kósmos

parole.significato: Preparations applied externally to change or enhance the beauty of skin, hair, nails, lips, and eyes.
parole.testo: From French cosmétique, from Ancient Greek κοσμητική (kosmētikḗ, “the art of dress and ornament”), from κοσμητικός (kosmētikós), an adjective of κοσμέω (kosméō, “to order, to arrange, to rule, to adorn, to equip, to dress, to embellish”).

parole.significato: To win prestige in battle by performing an act of bravery in the face of the enemy (such as touching him and escaping u…
parole.testo: count + coup (“quick, brilliant, and highly successful act”) (from French coup (“blow, hit, strike”), ultimately from Ancient Greek κόλᾰφος (kólăphos, “a buffet, a blow”)).

parole.significato: Relating to counterions.
parole.testo: From the suffix -cratic in words such as aristocratic, from French -cratique, from Ancient Greek -κρατικός (-kratikós). See -cratic for more.

parole.significato: A statue or other representation of a person carrying a ram.
parole.testo: From French, from Ancient Greek κριόφόρος (krióphóros, “carrying a ram”), from κριός (kriós, “ram”) + -φόρος (-phóros, “carrying”).

parole.significato: Hernial intrusion of the bladder into the vagina, resulting from tearing of the pubocervical fascia during childbirth a…
parole.testo: From French cystocèle, from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis, “anatomical sac”). By surface analysis, cysto- + -cele.

parole.significato: A fine-grained igneous rock composed mostly of pyroxene and feldspar.
parole.testo: From French diabase, from Ancient Greek διάβασις (diábasis).

parole.significato: Instructive or intended to teach or demonstrate, especially with regard to morality.
parole.testo: From French didactique, from Ancient Greek διδακτικός (didaktikós, “skilled in teaching”), from διδακτός (didaktós, “taught, learnt”), from διδάσκω (didáskō, “to teach, educate”). By surface analysis, didact + -ic.

parole.significato: A monoclinic pyroxene mineral, a magnesium calcium silicate with the chemical formula CaMgSi₂O₆, found in igneous and m…
parole.testo: From French diopside, from Ancient Greek δίοψις (díopsis, “transparency”) + -ide.

parole.significato: A grey intrusive igneous rock composed mostly of plagioclase feldspar, biotite, hornblende and/or pyroxene.
parole.testo: From French diorite, invented by mineralogist Alexandre Brongniart (1770-1847), derived from Ancient Greek διορίζω (diorízō, “distinguish”), from δι- plus ὁρίζω (horízō, “to limit”).

parole.significato: A person, such as an ambassador, who is accredited to represent a government officially in its relations with other gov…
parole.testo: From French diplomate, a back-formation from diplomatique (“diplomatic”), ultimately from Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma, “double-folded document”).

parole.significato: A type of fine-grained basaltic rock.
parole.testo: From French dolérite, from Ancient Greek δολερός (dolerós, “deceitful, deceptive”), because it was easily confounded with diorite, + -ite.

parole.significato: The crab plover, Dromas ardeola, of North Africa.
parole.testo: From French, from Ancient Greek δρόμος (drómos, “running”). Doublet of dromos.

parole.significato: The science or logic of speed.
parole.testo: < French dromologie < Ancient Greek δρόμος (drómos, “race, running, racetrack, course, path”) + λόγος (lógos, “account, explanation, narrative”); term coined by the French philosopher Paul Virilio to discuss the importance of speed in warfare and communication. Equivalent to dromo- + -logy.

parole.significato: Changing; active; in motion.
parole.testo: From French dynamique, from Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dunamikós, “powerful”), from δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”), from δύναμαι (dúnamai, “I am able”).

parole.significato: A unit of force in the CGS system; the force required to accelerate a mass of one gram by one centimetre per second per…
parole.testo: From the French dyne, from the Ancient Greek δῠ́νᾰμῐς (dŭ́nămĭs, “force”).

parole.significato: Related to the edition of a work.
parole.testo: Via French ecdotique from Ancient Greek ἐκδοτικός (ekdotikós), relating to ἔκδοσις (ékdosis, literally “outgiving”) which amongst other things means “publishing”.

parole.significato: Selecting a mixture of what appears to be best of various doctrines, methods or styles.
parole.testo: From French éclectique, from Ancient Greek ἐκλεκτικός (eklektikós, “selective”), from ἐκλέγω (eklégō, “to pick, choose”), from ἐκ (ek, “out, from”) + λέγω (légō, “to choose, count”). Cognate to elect.

parole.significato: An angelic being from the Book of Enoch.
parole.testo: From French égrégore (“spirit of a group”), from the Ancient Greek substantive of ἐγρήγορος (egrḗgoros, “wakeful”) meaning watcher, angel in the Book of Enoch.

parole.significato: Producing internal secretions that are transported around the body by the bloodstream.
parole.testo: From French endocrine, from endo- + Ancient Greek κρίνω (krínō, “to separate, also to secrete”).

parole.significato: Building complex lateral burrow systems in all layers of the soil.
parole.testo: From French endogé + -ic. Endogé, first applied in the context of earthworms by Marcel Bouché (see anecic), is from Ancient Greek ἔνδον (éndon, “within, inside”) + γῆ (gê, “earth”), modelled after French épigé. By surface analysis, endo- + geo- + -ic.

parole.significato: The scientific study of insects, and (informal) of other arthropods (and occasionally other invertebrates).
parole.testo: From French entomologie, from Ancient Greek ἔντομον (éntomon, “insect”) + -logie (from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “-logy”)), equivalent to entomo- + -logy.

parole.significato: of or relating to the early period of the Stone Age marked by the use of eoliths.
parole.testo: From French éolithique; from Ancient Greek Ἠώς (Ēṓs, “dawn”) + λίθος (líthos, “stone”) + -ic. By surface analysis, eo- + lith- + -ic.

parole.significato: Living on the surface of the land.
parole.testo: From French épigé + -ic. Épigé, first applied in the context of earthworms by Marcel Bouché (see anecic), is from Ancient Greek ἐπίγειος (epígeios, “terrestrial”).

parole.significato: An occurrence of a disease or disorder in a population of non-human animals at a frequency higher than that expected in…
parole.testo: From French épizootique, animal equivalent of epidemic, from épizootie, irregularly formed from Ancient Greek ἐπί (epí) + ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”). parole.significato: an epic, saga
parole.testo: Borrowed from French épopée.

parole.significato: Abnormal excitement of a bodily organ or tissue.
parole.testo: From French éréthisme, from Ancient Greek ἐρεθισμός (erethismós), from ἐρεθίζειν (erethízein, “to irritate”).

parole.significato: An aggregate fruit comprised of achenes, drupelets, follicles, or berries.
parole.testo: From French étairion, from Ancient Greek ἑταιρείᾱ (hetaireíā, “association”).

parole.significato: A light spongy cubical bone at the root of the nose, forming much of the walls of the nasal cavity and part of those of…
parole.testo: Borrowing from French ethmoïde, from Ancient Greek ἠθμοειδής (ēthmoeidḗs, “like a strainer, perforated”), from ἠθμός (ēthmós, “strainer, sieve”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-form, -like”).

parole.significato: Of sounds, especially speech: demonstrating or possessing euphony; agreeable to the ear; pleasant-sounding.
parole.testo: From euphonical + -ous (suffix forming adjectives denoting possession or presence of a quality, commonly in abundance). parole.significato: A pronunciation of letters and syllables which is pleasing to the ear.
parole.testo: From French euphonie, from Ancient Greek εὐφωνία (euphōnía), from εὐ- (eu-, prefix meaning ‘good, well’) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound; (human) voice; discourse, speech”) (from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to say, speak”)) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming feminine abstract nouns). The English word is analysabl

parole.significato: Running or draining to the sea.
parole.testo: From French exorrhéisme (“drainage reaching the sea”). Compare exo- from Ancient Greek ἔξω (éxō, “outer; external”), and -ic (“pertaining to”).

parole.significato: That releases energy in the form of heat.
parole.testo: From French exothermique, from exo- (“outside”) + thermique (“of heat”), both ultimately from Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, exo- + -thermic.

parole.significato: A lighthouse
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fanal, from Ancient Greek φανάριον (phanárion).

parole.significato: The art of preparing and eating good food.
parole.testo: From French gastronomie, from Ancient Greek γαστρονομία (gastronomía), from γαστήρ (gastḗr, “stomach”) + νόμος (nómos, “knowledge, law”); by surface analysis, gastro- (“cooking”) + -nomy (“a system of rules or laws about a particular field”).

parole.significato: A simple monosaccharide (sugar) with a molecular formula of C₆H₁₂O₆; a principle source of energy for cellular metaboli…
parole.testo: From French, from Ancient Greek γλεῦκος (gleûkos, “wine, must”). By surface analysis, gluco- + -ose; note that -ose is derived from the word glucose.

parole.significato: A figure carved in relief or incised, especially representing a sound, word, or idea.
parole.testo: First attested in 1727. Borrowed from French glyphe, from Ancient Greek γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carving”), from γλύφω (glúphō, “I carve, engrave”).

parole.significato: A room or building devoted to displaying works of sculpture.
parole.testo: From French glyptothèque, from Ancient Greek γλυπτός (gluptós, “carved, engraved”) + Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “box or chest”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to gnomes (sententious sayings).
parole.testo: From French gnomique, ultimately from Ancient Greek γνωμικός (gnōmikós), from γνώμη (gnṓmē, “thought, judgement”), akin to γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “know”). By surface analysis, gnome + -ic.

parole.significato: A unit of mass equal to one-thousandth of a kilogram. Symbol: g.
parole.testo: From French gramme, from Ancient Greek γράμμα (grámma, “a small weight, a scruple”). Doublet of gramma.

parole.significato: The study of, or the branch of medicine specializing in, the medical problems of women, especially disorders of the rep…
parole.testo: From French gynécologie, from Ancient Greek γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”, stem γυναικ-) + -logie (“-logy”). Replaced earlier gyniatrics.

parole.significato: A unit of surface area (symbol ㏊) equal to 100 ares (that is, 10,000 square metres, one hundredth of a square kilometre…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hectare, formed from Ancient Greek ἑκατόν (hekatón, “hundred”) + are, equivalent to hect- + are.

parole.significato: hundred
parole.testo: From French hecto-, from Ancient Greek ἑκατόν (hekatón, “hundred”). Doublet of hecato- and centi-.

parole.significato: A thing having seven parts or divisions.
parole.testo: From French heptaméride, from Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”) + French méride (compare meridian).

parole.significato: The branch of biology dealing with reptiles (Reptilia) and amphibians (Amphibia).
parole.testo: Derived from French herpétologie, from Ancient Greek ἑρπετόν (herpetón, “reptile”) + -logie (suffix indicating a field of study or work), equivalent to herpet- + -logy.

parole.significato: A physical manifestation of the holy or sacred, serving as a spiritual eidolon for emulation or worship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hiérophanie, as used by Romanian religious historian and philosopher Mircea Eliade (1907–1986) in his book The Sacred and the Profane (1959; translated into English from an unpublished French original), from Ancient Greek ἱερός (hierós, “sacred, holy sign”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “sho

parole.significato: a mythical beast, half griffin and half horse, supposedly the offspring of a griffin and a filly.
parole.testo: From French hippogriffe, from Ancient Greek ἵππος (híppos, “horse”, English hippo-) + γρύψ (grúps, “griffin”).

parole.significato: Relating to the tissues of the body.
parole.testo: 19th century. From French histique, from Ancient Greek ἱστός (histós, “web”).

parole.significato: Of a geologic epoch within the Quaternary period from about the year 10 000 BC to the present; the age of man.
parole.testo: From French Holocène, based on holo- (“whole”) + Ancient Greek καινός (kainós, “fresh, new”). Coined to replace the earlier (1833) label Recent, formally submitted in 1867 and officially endorsed in 1969. The concept is that this epoch is entirely (wholly) new. By surface analysis, holo- + -cene.

parole.significato: Something homologous; a homologous organ or part, chemical compound, chromosome, gene, or cultural element.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French homologue, From Ancient Greek ὁμόλογος (homólogos, “agreeing, of one mind”), equivalent to homo- + -log.

parole.significato: A musical texture in which two or more parts move together in harmony, the relationship between them creating chords; t…
parole.testo: Internationalism, from French homophonie, from Ancient Greek ὁμοφωνία (homophōnía, “unison”), from ὁμόφωνος (homóphōnos, “of the same sound or tone”). By surface analysis, homo- + -phony.

parole.significato: The science of health, its promotion and preservation.
parole.testo: From French hygiène, from Ancient Greek ὑγιεινή (τέχνη) (hugieinḗ (tékhnē), literally “art of health”), from ὑγιεινός (hugieinós, “of health, good for the health, wholesome, sound, healthy”), from ὑγιής (hugiḗs, “healthy, sound”).

parole.significato: An increase in the size of an organ or tissue due to the enlargement of its individual cells.
parole.testo: From French hypertrophie, from Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “over, excessive”) + τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment”), equivalent to hyper- + -trophy.

parole.significato: That induces sleep; soporific, somniferous.
parole.testo: From French hypnagogique, from Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “leading”).

parole.significato: Related to, or affected by hypochondria.
parole.testo: From French hypocondriaque, from Ancient Greek ὑποχονδριακός (hupokhondriakós, “of the region between the ribs and navel”), from ὑποχόνδριος (hupokhóndrios, “the space between the ribs and the navel”), from ὑπό (hupó, “below”) + χόνδρος (khóndros, “cartilage”). See also hypochondrium, hypochondria,

parole.significato: A government characterized by incompetent leaders.
parole.testo: From inept, from French inepte (“feckless”) + -o- + -cracy, from Ancient Greek κράτος (krátos, “strength, power”).

parole.significato: Synonym of iodine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French iode.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol: I) with an atomic number of 53; one of the halogens.
parole.testo: From French iode + -ine, from Ancient Greek ἰοειδής (ioeidḗs, “violet”). Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1814.

parole.significato: isocheimal
parole.testo: From French isochimène, from iso- + Ancient Greek χειμαίνω (kheimaínō, “to be wintry”), from χεῖμα (kheîma, “winter”).

parole.significato: An isotherm connecting points on a map with equal mean summer temperature.
parole.testo: From French isothère, from iso- + Ancient Greek θέρος (théros, “summer”).

parole.significato: A line on a graph or chart, such as a weather map, along which all the points have the same temperature.
parole.testo: From the French isotherme (“of equal temperature”, adjective), itself from Ancient Greek ἴσος (ísos, “equal”) + θέρμη (thérmē, “warmth”). By surface analysis, iso- + -therm.

parole.significato: A hard raised growth of scar tissue at the site of an injury.
parole.testo: 19th century, from French chéloïde, from Ancient Greek χηλή (khēlḗ, “hoof”) and -oid.

parole.significato: Inflammation of the cornea.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from French kératite, from Ancient Greek κέρᾰτ- (kérăt-), κέρας (kéras, “horn”) + French -ite (“-itis”); see kerato-.

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French kilo-, irregularly derived from Ancient Greek χίλιοι (khílioi, “one thousand”). parole.significato: The branch of mechanics concerned with objects in motion, but not with the forces involved.
parole.testo: French cinématique, from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, “motion”) + -ics.

parole.significato: The principal phospholipid in animals; it is particularly abundant in egg yolks, and is extracted commercially from soy…
parole.testo: From French lécithine, coined in 1847 by Theodore Gobley, from Ancient Greek λέκιθος (lékithos, “egg yolk”).

parole.significato: A black iron-potash mica, usually found in granitic rocks in small six-sided tables, or as an aggregation of minute opa…
parole.testo: French [Term?], from Ancient Greek [Term?].

parole.significato: One who writes or compiles a dictionary.
parole.testo: From French lexicographe + -er, from Ancient Greek λεξικός (lexikós, “of words”) + γράφω (gráphō, “write”). By surface analysis, lexico- + -grapher.

parole.significato: A minimal unit of reading, such as a sentence or sentence fragment
parole.testo: From the French lexie, originating in the writings of Roland Barthes. Further from Ancient Greek λέξῐς (léxĭs, “a saying, a word”).

parole.significato: Relating to symbolic logic.
parole.testo: From French logistique, from Ancient Greek λογιστικός (logistikós, “practiced in arithmetic; rational”), from λογίζομαι (logízomai, “I reason, I calculate”), from λόγος (lógos, “reason, computation”), whence English logos, logic, logarithm, etc.; modern mathematical use influenced by related logarit

parole.significato: Pertaining to motion at a constant angle to the meridians; on a set compass bearing.
parole.testo: From French loxodromique, from Ancient Greek λοξός (loxós, “oblique”) + δρόμος (drómos, “course”).

parole.significato: large
parole.testo: From French, from Latin, from Ancient Greek μακρο- (makro-), combinging form of μακρός (makrós, “long”). By surface analysis, macr- + -o-.

parole.significato: The study of molluscs.
parole.testo: From French malacologie, contraction of malacozoologie, from the (obsolete) taxonomic name Malacozoa + French -ologie (“-ology”), Malacozoa being in turn from Ancient Greek μαλακός (malakós, “soft”) + ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”). Equivalent to malaco- + -logy.

parole.significato: An instrument to measure pressure in a fluid, especially a double-legged liquid column gauge used to measure the differ…
parole.testo: From French manomètre, formed from Ancient Greek μανός (manós, “thin, rare”) + μέτρον (métron), equivalent to mano- + -meter.

parole.significato: A 42.195-kilometre (26-mile-385-yard) road race.
parole.testo: From French marathon, coined in 1894 by linguist Michel Bréal for the first modern time Olympic Games after Ancient Greek Μαραθών (Marathṓn), a town northeast of Athens. parole.significato: Pertaining to pearl or pearls (rare except in the designation of margaric acid)
parole.testo: From French margarique (in acide margarique), ultimately from Ancient Greek μάργαρον (márgaron, “pearl”).

parole.significato: A spread, manufactured from a blend of vegetable oils (some of which are hydrogenated), emulsifiers etc, mostly used as…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French margarine, from acide margarique (“margaric acid”), from Ancient Greek μάργαρον (márgaron, “pearl”), in allusion to its pearly lustre, with the suffix -ine, influenced by glycérine (“glycerine”). parole.significato: A macrocosm.
parole.testo: From French mégacosme, ultimately from Ancient Greek μεγα- (mega-) + κόσμος (kósmos).

parole.significato: Various dark-coloured volcanic igneous rocks rich in augite, similar to and in some definitions including basalt, princ…
parole.testo: French, from Ancient Greek, meaning "black porphyry".

parole.significato: A yellow clay mineral from Bavaria.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mélinite, from Ancient Greek μήλινος (mḗlinos, “quince-yellow”).

parole.significato: Synonym of raffinose.
parole.testo: From French mélitose, from Ancient Greek μέλιτ- (mélit-, “honey”) + French -ose.

parole.significato: Music.
parole.testo: From French mélo-, from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb, musical phrase, melody, song, tune”).

parole.significato: A kind of drama having a musical accompaniment to intensify the effect of certain scenes.
parole.testo: From French mélodrame, the second element refashioned by analogy with drama; ultimately from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “limb”, “member”, “song”, “tune”, “melody”) + δρᾶμα (drâma, “deed”, “theatrical act”). Compare melodrame. Cognate to German Melodram and Spanish melodrama.

parole.significato: A wise and trusted counselor or teacher.
parole.testo: From French mentor, from Ancient Greek Μέντωρ (Méntōr, “Mentor”), a mythological character in the Odyssey, whose name, a historical name from Ancient Greece, shares the same root as English mind. Cognate to Sanskrit मन्तृ (mantṛ, “advisor, counselor”) and Latin monitor (“one who admonishes”), and pe

parole.significato: A flat, sharp-edged button, often a disc-shaped knob, separating the stem of a drinking-glass from the foot.
parole.testo: Perhaps via French [Term?] (compare French mérèse (growth by cell division), mérisme (merismus, merism)), ultimately from Ancient Greek μερίζω (merízō), from μέρος (méros, “part”) + -ίζω (-ízō, “-ize”), from Proto-Hellenic *(h)méros. First English attestation in 1923 on page 44 of Glass-making in En

parole.significato: A colony of plastids.
parole.testo: From French méride from Ancient Greek μερίς (merís, “a part”).

parole.significato: Any of three species of bird in the family Mesitornithidae within the order Mesitornithiformes, endemic to Madagascar.
parole.testo: From French mésite (“mesite”), named by the zoologist Isidore Geoffroy in 1838. Perhaps from Ancient Greek μεσίτης (mesítēs, “mediator”), for these birds are of medium size.

parole.significato: A submersible submarine designed for drifting on sea currents in the middle depth layers of the ocean.
parole.testo: From French mésoscaphe. From meso- + Ancient Greek σκάφη (skáphē, “little ship”). Coined by Jacques Piccard.

parole.significato: The science of metals; their extraction from ores, purification and alloying, heat treatment, and working.
parole.testo: From French métallurgie, from Ancient Greek μεταλλουργός (metallourgós, “miner”).

parole.significato: The divalent group –CH₂– in which the free valencies are part of single bonds.
parole.testo: French méthylène, from Ancient Greek μέθυ (méthu, “wine”) + ὕλη (húlē, “wood”). By surface analysis, meth- + -ylene.

parole.significato: Divination by interpreting the facial lines and wrinkles, especially the forehead.
parole.testo: From French métopomantie (from Ancient Greek μέτωπον (métōpon, “forehead”)), later reformed after + -mancy.

parole.significato: The basic unit of length in the International System of Units (SI: Système International d'Unités), equal to the distan…
parole.testo: From French mètre, from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, “measure, rule, length, size, poetic metre”). Doublet of meter, metron, and mether.

parole.significato: Any microorganism; (loosely, nonscientifically) especially, a harmful bacterium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French microbe, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) and βίος (bíos, “life”). By surface analysis, micro- + -obe.

parole.significato: Having an abnormally small head.
parole.testo: From French microcéphalique, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

parole.significato: Synonym of micrometre (“one-millionth of a metre”).
parole.testo: From French micron, from Ancient Greek μικρόν (mikrón), neuter of μικρός (mikrós, “small”).

parole.significato: In seed-bearing plants, a small opening in the integuments of the ovule through which sperm are able to access the ovum.
parole.testo: From French, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + πύλη (púlē, “gate”).

parole.significato: A short humorous dramatic scene in verse.
parole.testo: From mimiambus, possibly from French mimiambe, from Ancient Greek μιμιάμβους (mimiámbous, “mime-iamb”), from μῖμος (mîmos, “actor, imitator”) + ἴαμβος (íambos, “iamb”).

parole.significato: a canoe or boat made from a single piece of timber
parole.testo: From French monoxyle, from Ancient Greek μονόξυλον (monóxulon).

parole.significato: A philosophical or learned fool.
parole.testo: From obsolete French morosophe, from Ancient Greek μωρόσοφος (mōrósophos), from μωρός (mōrós, “dull, stupid”) + σοφός (sophós, “wise”).

parole.significato: The smallest linguistic unit within a word that can carry a meaning. It may be a letter, a syllable, or otherwise.
parole.testo: From French morphème. Ultimately from Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “shape, form”). By surface analysis, morph + -eme.

parole.significato: innumerable: myriad, myriapod
parole.testo: From French myria-, ultimately from Ancient Greek μυρίος (muríos, “ten thousand”).

parole.significato: To thoroughly confuse, befuddle, or bewilder.
parole.testo: From French mystifier, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”) + Latin -ficare.

parole.significato: A disorder characterized by sudden and uncontrollable attacks of deep sleep, often brief, sometimes accompanied by para…
parole.testo: From French narcolepsie. By surface analysis, narco- + -lepsy, from Ancient Greek ναρκόω (narkóō, “put to sleep”) + λῆψις (lêpsis, “seizure”).

parole.significato: A word or phrase which has recently been coined; a new word or phrase.
parole.testo: From French néologisme, from Ancient Greek νέος (néos, “new”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”) + -ism.

parole.significato: A prefecture or unit of regional government in Greece.
parole.testo: From French nome, from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “district”), from νέμω (némō, “to divide”). Doublet of nomos.

parole.significato: A term in an algebraic expression.
parole.testo: The sense "term" is from French -nôme, second element of binôme etc., again from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós) here in its sense "division". The name of the special function may be identical or may be an independent borrowing from the Greek.

parole.significato: The sphere of human reason, thought, and consciousness, seen as a theoretical evolutionary stage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French noosphère, from Ancient Greek νόος (nóos, “mind, spirit”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”), developed and perhaps coined by Pierre Teilhard de Chardin and Vladimir Vernadsky, in analogy to atmosphere, biosphere etc. By surface analysis, nous (“mind”) + -sphere.

parole.significato: Synonym of octapla.
parole.testo: From French octaples, from Ancient Greek ὀκταπλά (oktaplá), neuter plural of ὀκταπλοῦς (oktaploûs, “eightfold”), from ὀκτα- (okta-, “octa-: eight”) + -πλόος (-plóos, “-fold”), used as the title of such an edition by Origen.

parole.significato: An instrument, usually embedded within the speedometer of a vehicle, that measures the distance the vehicle has travele…
parole.testo: From French odomètre, from Ancient Greek ὁδός (hodós, “road, path, way”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”), equivalent to odo- + -meter.

parole.significato: The scapula.
parole.testo: From French omoplate, from Ancient Greek ὠμοπλάτη (ōmoplátē, “shoulder blade”), from ὦμος (ômos, “shoulder”) + πλάτη (plátē, “something flat or broad”). By surface analysis, omo- (“shoulder”) + plate.

parole.significato: The branch of lexicology devoted to the study of names and naming, especially the origins of names.
parole.testo: First attested in 1936, from the adjective onomastic (“of or belonging to naming”) (1716) with a suffix -s, from French onomastique, from Ancient Greek ὀνομαστικός (onomastikós), from ὀνομαστός (onomastós, “named”), form of ὀνομάζω (onomázō, “I name”), from ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”), from Proto-Indo-Eur

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the sensory properties of a particular food or chemical, the taste, colour, odour, and feel.
parole.testo: From French organoleptique, from organo- + Ancient Greek ληπτικός (lēptikós, “disposed to take”), from λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”).

parole.significato: An aircraft that generates lift through the flapping of its wings.
parole.testo: From French ornithoptère, from Ancient Greek ὄρνιθ- (órnith-) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing”), equivalent to ornitho- + -pter.

parole.significato: The process of mountain building by the upward folding of the Earth's crust.
parole.testo: From French orogénie, from Ancient Greek ὄρος (óros, “mountain, high ground”) + γενεια (geneia, “creation, birth, making”). By surface analysis, oro- + -geny.

parole.significato: An alloy of copper and zinc or tin that has a gold color, used in making inexpensive jewelry.
parole.testo: From French, from or (“gold”) + Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos, “appearance”, “shape”, “form”).

parole.significato: Synonym of otolith.
parole.testo: A Latinised adaptation (taking the form of a Latin second-declension neuter noun in the nominative case, as if from a Latin *ōtoconium) of the French otoconie (whence otocony, otokony), itself formed from the Ancient Greek οὖς, ὠτ- (oûs, ōt-, “ot-; ear”) + κονία (konía, “dust”).

parole.significato: Concerning oxygen
parole.testo: Reduced from oxygen which in turn is from French oxygène, from Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús).

parole.significato: A formal speech publicly praising someone or something.
parole.testo: From French panégyrique, from Ancient Greek πανηγυρικός (panēgurikós).

parole.significato: A mechanical linkage based on parallelograms causing two objects to move in parallel; notably as a drawing aid.
parole.testo: From French pantographe, from panto- (from Ancient Greek παντός (pantós), genitive singular of πᾶν (pân, “all”)), and -graphe (from γράφειν (gráphein, “to write”)).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a paradigm.
parole.testo: From French paradigmatique, from Ancient Greek πᾰρᾰδειγμᾰτῐκός (părădeigmătĭkós).

parole.significato: a universal language
parole.testo: From French pasilalie, formed from Ancient Greek πᾶς (pâs, “all”) + λαλιά (laliá, “speech, dialect”).

parole.significato: An absurdist philosophy or pseudoscience studying things "beyond" metaphysics.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pataphysique, where it was coined by author Alfred Jarry from a pun deriving from the Ancient Greek title of a work by Aristotle; see pataphysique for more.

parole.significato: A plant-derived polysaccharide found in cell walls (especially in fruits) that forms a gel under acidic conditions and…
parole.testo: From French pectine, coined in the 1830s by Henri Braconnot, from acide pectique "pectic acid", from Ancient Greek πηκτικός (pēktikós, “curdling”), from πηκτός (pēktós, “curdled”), from πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “stiffen”).

parole.significato: A man who is engaged in an erotic relationship with an adolescent boy; a practitioner of pederasty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pédéraste, from Ancient Greek παιδεραστής (paiderastḗs, “lover of boys”), from παῖς (paîs, “boy”) and ἐραστής (erastḗs, “lover”).

parole.significato: The external smooth horny layer of a hoof.
parole.testo: French périople, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The fibula.
parole.testo: From French péroné, from Ancient Greek περόνη (perónē, “fibula”).

parole.significato: A rock carving, especially one made in prehistoric times.
parole.testo: From French pétroglyphe, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “rock”) + γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carved work”). By surface analysis, petro- + glyph.

parole.significato: phantasmagoria
parole.testo: From French phantasmagorie, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma, “ghost”) + ἀγορεύω (agoreúō, “to speak publicly”).

parole.significato: An early animation device consisting of a disc or drum which rotated, showing successive images through slits, often vi…
parole.testo: From French phénakistiscope, from Ancient Greek φενακιστής (phenakistḗs, “cheat, imposter”) + French -scope.

parole.significato: Benzene.
parole.testo: Proposed 1836 by French scientist Auguste Laurent as an alternative name for benzene, from French phène, from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaínō, “bring to light, cause to appear, show”).

parole.significato: A caustic, poisonous, white crystalline compound, C₆H₅OH, derived from benzene and used in resins, plastics, and pharma…
parole.testo: From French phène, from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaínō, “to clear”), as it was used for illumination, name given by Auguste Laurente in 1836. By surface analysis, pheno- + -ol.

parole.significato: Stamp collecting.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1865. Borrowed from French philatélie, coined by French stamp collector Georges Herpin in 1864 (in Le Collectionneur de Timbres-poste, Nov. 15, 1864), from Ancient Greek φιλέω (philéō, “I love”) + ἀτέλεια (atéleia), the closest word he could find in Ancient Greek to the concept

parole.significato: Synonym of kaolinite.
parole.testo: From French pholérite, equivalent to Ancient Greek φολίς (pholís) + -ite.

parole.significato: An association between two organisms in which one (e.g. a mite) travels on the body of another, without being a parasit…
parole.testo: From French phorésie, from Ancient Greek φόρησις (phórēsis, “wearing, garment”), from φορέω (phoréō, “I wear, I bear”) + -σις (-sis, nominal suffix). See -phore.

parole.significato: A sensation of lights induced by mechanical, electrical, or magnetic stimulation (rather than optical) of the retina or…
parole.testo: From French phosphène, from Ancient Greek φῶς (phôs, “light”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to appear, shine”).

parole.significato: Designating a type of bitter yellow acid.
parole.testo: From French picrique, from Ancient Greek πικρός (pikrós, “bitter”).

parole.significato: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, C₆H₂(NO₂)₃, prepared by the nitration of phenol or of aspirin; a toxic, yellow, explosive substan…
parole.testo: From French picrique, from Ancient Greek πικρός (pikrós, “bitter”).

parole.significato: A person who writes in support of one opinion, doctrine, or system, in opposition to another; one skilled in polemics;…
parole.testo: From French polémique, from Ancient Greek πολεμικός (polemikós, “of war”), from πόλεμος (pólemos, “war”). By surface analysis, polem- + -ic.

parole.significato: The explicit literary or visual depiction of sexual subject matter; any display of material of an erotic nature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pornographie. By surface analysis, porno- + -graphy.

parole.significato: Denoting the presence of 3 carbon atoms in the parent chain when forming names of organic compounds.
parole.testo: By false splitting from propionic or directly from French propionique. Ultimately from Ancient Greek πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”) and πίων (píōn, “fat”).

parole.significato: The frequently specialised or reduced leaf produced at the first node of a new shoot.
parole.testo: Originally coined by French botanists, from Ancient Greek πρό (pró) and φύλλον (phúllon).

parole.significato: The compound with the formula CH₃CH₂COOH, a naturally occurring carboxylic acid with a pungent odor.
parole.testo: From French acide propionique, coined by chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas, from Ancient Greek πρῶτος (prôtos) ("first") and πίων (píōn) ("fat"), because it was the smallest carboxylic acid that exhibited the properties of the other fatty acids, such as producing an oily layer when salted out of water and

parole.significato: A gastropod with gills in front of the heart, formerly thought to belong to a single group, Prosobranchia.
parole.testo: From French prosobranche, from Ancient Greek πρόσω (prósō, “forwards”) + βράγχια (bránkhia, “gills”). By surface analysis, proso- + -branch.

parole.significato: A form of granite containing silvery flakes of talc or similar minerals.
parole.testo: From French protogine, coined in 1806 on the basis of Ancient Greek πρωτόγονος (prōtógonos, “first-created”), with an added suffix -ine, which the author used for certain minerals.

parole.significato: A fictitious name (more literally, a false name), as those used by writers and movie stars.
parole.testo: Back-formation from pseudonymous, from French pseudonyme (“pseudonymous”, adjective), from Ancient Greek ψευδώνυμος (pseudṓnumos), from ψευδής (pseudḗs, “false”) and ὄνυμα (ónuma), a dialectal form of ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”). By surface analysis, pseudo- + -onym.

parole.significato: The point corresponding with the posterior end of the sphenoparietal suture; known as the weakest part of the skull.
parole.testo: From French ptérion, from ptère (“wing of the sphenoid bone”) + -ion, from Ancient Greek πτερόν (pterón, “wing”).

parole.significato: A pterosaur of the genus Pterodactylus.
parole.testo: From French ptérodactyle, a term coined by Cuvier from Ancient Greek πτερόν (pterón, “wing”) + δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”). By surface analysis, ptero- + -dactyl.

parole.significato: Any of a group of crystalline minerals containing silicates of iron, magnesium and calcium.
parole.testo: From French pyroxène, from pyro- + Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “stranger”).

parole.significato: A dissecting instrument for opening the spinal canal.
parole.testo: From French rachitome, from Ancient Greek ῥάχις (rhákhis, “the spine”) + τομός (tomós, “to cut”).

parole.significato: Divination by reading a random passage from a poem.
parole.testo: From French rhapsodomancie, from Ancient Greek ῥαψῳδός (rhapsōidós) + -mancy.

parole.significato: Any of the free-swimming tunicates of the order Salpida and its single family Salpidae.
parole.testo: From French salpe, from Ancient Greek σᾰ́λπη (sắlpē, “porgy”). Doublet of salpa.

parole.significato: Any carangoid fish of the genus Trachurus, especially Trachurus trachurus, of Europe and America, and Trachurus pictura…
parole.testo: From French French saurel (“jack mackerel”), from Ancient Greek σαῦρος (saûros, “horse mackerel”). Compare Spanish jurel.

parole.significato: A single-reed instrument musical instrument of the woodwind family, usually made of brass and with a distinctive loop b…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French saxophone, a combination of the surname of its inventor Adolphe Sax (1814–1894) + -o- + -phone (“something that makes a sound”), from Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound, voice”). The first element surname is a variant of the German Sachs (“Saxon”). Analyzable as Sax + -o- + -phon

parole.significato: A lunar eclipse occurring as the Moon sets, simultaneously with sunrise.
parole.testo: French coinage, from the Ancient Greek σελήνη (selḗnē, “moon”) and ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”).

parole.significato: A nonmetallic chemical element (symbol Se) with an atomic number of 34, used mainly in glassmaking and pigments and as…
parole.testo: From French sélénium, the name coined by Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1818 from Ancient Greek σελήνη (selḗnē, “moon”) in reference to original confusion with the similar element tellurium.

parole.significato: A branch of linguistics studying the meaning of words.
parole.testo: From French sémantique, displacing earlier semasiology. From Ancient Greek σημαντικός (sēmantikós). By surface analysis, semantic + -ics.

parole.significato: Any equipment used for visual signalling by means of flags, lights, or mechanically moving arms, which are used to repr…
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from French sémaphore, from Ancient Greek σῆμα (sêma, “mark, sign, token”) + French -phore (from Ancient Greek -φόρος (-phóros, suffix indicating a bearer or carrier)). By surface analysis, sema- + -phore. The verb is derived from the noun.

parole.significato: A coil of wire that acts as a magnet when an electric current flows through it.
parole.testo: From French solénoïde, from Ancient Greek σωληνοειδής (sōlēnoeidḗs) (from σωλήν (sōlḗn, “channel, pipe”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs); see -oid).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the star Sirius, particularly in Egyptian or ancient Greek contexts.
parole.testo: From Sothis (“Sirius”) + -ic (forming adjectives), a variant of earlier Sothiac, from French sothiaque, ultimately from Ancient Greek σωθιακός (sōthiakós, “Sothic”), from Σῶθις (Sôthis, “Sirius”) and -κός (-kós, “-ic”, forming adjectives).

parole.significato: titanite
parole.testo: From French sphène, coined by René Just Haüy in 1801, Traité de minéralogie vol. 3 p. 114, after Ancient Greek σφήν (sphḗn, “wedge”).

parole.significato: Solid fat.
parole.testo: From French stéarine, from Ancient Greek στέαρ (stéar, “fat”).

parole.significato: The central core of a plant's root and stem system, especially including the vascular tissue and developed from the ple…
parole.testo: From 1886 French stèle, from Ancient Greek στήλη (stḗlē, “upright rock; pillar; column”).

parole.significato: A measure of volume used e.g. for cut wood, equal to one cubic metre.
parole.testo: From French stère, from Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós, “solid”), because the unit was used for solid commodities such as firewood.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a syntagma.
parole.testo: From French syntagmatique, from Ancient Greek συνταγμᾰτικός (suntagmătikós).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to synthesis.
parole.testo: From French synthétique, from Ancient Greek συνθετικός (sunthetikós); Equivalent to synthesis + -ic (suffix formation of -tic).

parole.significato: The practical aspects of a given art, occupation etc.; formal requirements.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French technique (“technicality; branch of knowledge”), noun use of technique (“technical”), from Ancient Greek τεχνικός (tekhnikós, “of or pertaining to art, artistic, skilful”), from τέχνη (tékhnē, “art, handicraft”). Doublet of technic.

parole.significato: Synonym of tetrapla.
parole.testo: From French tétraples, from Ancient Greek τετραπλᾶ (tetraplâ), neuter plural of τετραπλοῦς (tetraploûs, “fourfold”), from τετρα- (tetra-, “tetra-: four”) + -πλόος (-plóos, “-fold”).

parole.significato: of or relating to seas and oceans
parole.testo: From French thalassique, from Ancient Greek θάλασσα (thálassa, “sea”) + -ique.

parole.significato: A justification of a deity or of particular attributes of a deity; specifically, a justification of the existence of ev…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French théodicée, from Ancient Greek θεός (theós, “god”) + δίκη (díkē, “justice”), coined by German mathematician and philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in his 1710 work Essais de Théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu, la liberté de l'homme et l'origine du mal (Essays of Theodicy on the Go

parole.significato: A counterrevolution; a coup d'état resembling the Thermidorian Reaction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French thermidor, from Ancient Greek θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) + δῶρον (dôron, “gift”).

parole.significato: The quality of a sound independent of its pitch and volume.
parole.testo: From French timbre, ultimately from Ancient Greek τύμπανον (túmpanon, “drum”). Doublet of tympanum, timpani, timbal, and tymbal.

parole.significato: A pale igneous rock consisting mostly of potassium feldspar and plagioclase.
parole.testo: From French trachyte, from Ancient Greek τρᾱχύς (trākhús, “rough”).

parole.significato: The slender, hair-like cell which receives the fertilizing particles, or antherozoids, in female red algae, lichens and…
parole.testo: French, from Ancient Greek θρίξ (thríx, “hair”) + γυνή (gunḗ, “female”)

parole.significato: In vertebrates with legs, the end of the femur near the hip joint, not including the head or neck.
parole.testo: From French trochanter, from Ancient Greek τροχαντήρ (trokhantḗr).

parole.significato: The lesser tuberosity of the head of the humerus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French trochin, from troch(anter) + -in, from Ancient Greek τροχαντήρ (trokhantḗr), from τροχάνη (trokhánē, “wheel, axle, gear”) + -τήρ (-tḗr), from τροχάζω (trokházō, “to run quickly”).

parole.significato: The greater tuberosity of the humerus, admitting several of the muscles of the shoulders.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French trochiter, from Ancient Greek τροχαντήρ (trokhantḗr).

parole.significato: The water-soluble part of the yellow carotenoid pigment present in the cell sap of some plants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French xantheine, apparently an arbitrary respelling to distinguish it from the similarly spelled xanthine. Ultimately from Ancient Greek; see xanthine. By surface analysis, xanth- + -ein.

parole.significato: Any of a group of alkaloids that include caffeine, theophylline, and theobromine as well as the parent compound, a prec…
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, from French xanthine, reflecting New Latin combining forms: xanth- + -ine; ultimately from Ancient Greek ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”), because xanthine is yellowish-white. By surface analysis, xanth- + -ine.

parole.significato: A word used in utterances of a language but generally marked as foreign.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French xénisme, from Ancient Greek ξενισμός (xenismós, “strangeness, novelty”).

parole.significato: The intimate pairing of homologous chromosomes during the synaptic stage of meiosis
parole.testo: From French zygotène, corresponding to zygo- (“union, zygosis”, from Ancient Greek ζυγόν (zugón, “junction, yoke”)) + -tene (“filament”, from ταινία (tainía, “band, fillet”)), equivalent to zygote + -tene. Coined by Victor Grégoire in 1907 and in English by Edmund B. Wilson in 1912.
